title: MC0-09327
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: Mr. XXXX and Ms. XXXX, you and your children are citizens of Angola, and you state that you fear persecution in your country, when your in-laws, Sir, wanted your eldest daughter to marry one of your uncles, Madam, which you refused. As a result, the in-laws became violent and sent criminals to threaten you.1
Sir, you are acting as the designated representative of your minor children.2
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected your refugee protection claims after finding that you were not credible.3
On appeal, you submitted evidence, requested that an oral hearing be held and argue that the RPD committed errors regarding your credibility.4

After analyzing your file, I concluded that the documentary evidence submitted on appeal was not admissible and that it was impossible to hold a hearing. I also concluded that the RPD did not commit the errors you criticize it for.
In light of these conclusions, your appeal is dismissed.

The Rules of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD Rules) set out that the person who is the subject of the appeal must provide in his memorandum full and detailed submissions of how any documentary evidence that he wants to raise on appeal meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and how that evidence relates to the appellant.5

In your written statement, Mr. XXXX, you state that you submitted evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA,6 which are included in written testimony.7 In your memorandum, you argue that this written testimony satisfies the requirements of subsection 110(4) because they were obtained after the hearing before the RPD and that at the time of that hearing, none of the in-laws had dared testify about this situation out of fear of retaliation. You also submit that you had to convince this cousin so that he would agree to testify and that this testimony has a tie to you because he is your wife's cousin and that he had been aware of this situation since the start until now.8

I find it necessary to point out that subsection 110(3) of the IRPA explicitly sets out that, generally, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the RPD. Subsection 110(4) creates an exception to this general rule. The existence of criteria governing the admissibility of new evidence on appeal helps to preserve the integrity of the process by promoting finality with respect to the factual record at the first level of decision-making, with very limited exceptions, and encouraging the narrowing of issues as matters move up the appellate ladder.9

In the written testimony dated XXXX 19, 2020, your cousin, Ms. XXXX, states that he witnessed the troubling events that your uncle, XXXX XXXX, committed in your home; the problems and death threats had begun in 2010 after you and your husband refused this uncle's request to marry your then eight-year-old daughter. He also states that in XXXX 2015, you were violently threatened at night by a group of criminals with firearms and blades. The uncle was a member of the group. Each member of this group wore a balaclava so that their faces were covered. Their goal was to kill you, Mr. XXXX, but you managed to escape. Your cousin also states that the criminals spent their anger by stabbing you, Ms. XXXX, thus causing serious injuries to your feet. Lastly, your cousin states that, since that time, your house, Ms. XXXX, has become the criminals' open target of threats. Before signing, your cousin states that, in the past, he did not want to testify because he wanted to avoid any conflict with the uncle.

In my opinion, this written testimony from your cousin concerns primarily facts that arose before the RPD rejected your refugee protection claims. Although he states that when he signed this testimony, your house was the criminals' open target, your cousin did not add any specific information to this matter. Just the same, you yourself stated before the RPD that these criminals were still looking for you. Furthermore, in considering the source of this testimony and the circumstances in which it came to light, namely after the RPD's rejection of your refugee protection claims, I find that this testimony lacks credibility.10

Consequently, while being aware that your cousin states that he was unable to testify earlier, I conclude that this testimony is aimed at mainly confirming facts and allegations that have already been analyzed by the RPD, that credibility was lacking and there is no reason to admit it into evidence in your appeal.
The RAD Rules set out that the person who is the subject of the appeal must include in his memorandum full and detailed submissions regarding why the Division should hold a hearing.11
paragraphs.heading_before: II. AN ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: In your memorandum, you submitted that the written testimony from this cousin puts things in context regarding your credibility and he corroborates what you, Mr. XXXX, stated at the hearing, namely that you were persecuted by your in-laws for refusing the marriage proposal to your then eight-year-old daughter from an uncle who was 38 years old at the time.12

It is up to the RAD to determine whether the criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA are satisfied or not.13 One of the criteria set out in this subsection is that the evidence submitted on appeal must be found admissible. However, I found that the evidence you submitted in your appeal is not admissible. Consequently, it is not possible to hold a hearing.14 III.

The role of the RAD is not to conduct a de novo consideration of a claim for refugee protection, but rather to determine whether the RPD erred as alleged. 15 I have conducted an independent analysis of your record, and I am of the opinion that the correctness standard of review must be applied.16 A. The errors committed by the Refugee Protection Division according to you

The RAD Rules stipulate that the person who is the subject of the appeal must specify: i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, and ii) where the errors are located in the RPD decision, or in the transcript or in any recording of the hearing.17

When asked to explain the errors committed that make up the grounds of the appeal and to provide the full and detailed submissions regarding each error, the following is verbatim what your counsel writes on the matter: [translation] The panel is of the opinion that the appellants' allegations regarding the criminals whom the in-laws had sent after them undermine their credibility. However, the appellants clearly testified that it was indeed the female appellant's 38-year-old uncle who wanted to marry their eight-year-old daughter and that he had the in-laws' overall blessing, as nearly the entire family of the female appellant agreed to this marriage, and it was the in-laws who, unable to make them change their minds, got the criminals to go after them. The panel notes a major inconsistency that undermines the appellants' credibility when they state that there was a connection between the break-in and the uncle's threats. The appellants clearly stated that they were threatened by the in-laws because of their resistance to the marriage. It is only normal for them to establish a link between the break-in and the threats from the in-laws. The panel is of the opinion that the appellants' testimony was not sincere, or credible regarding the allegations of visits made by the uncle. The appellants clearly testified at the hearing as to the number of times they met with the uncle and that he often acted through others. The panel itself recognized that the appellants were the victims of a break-in with photographic evidence of scars. This situation does not come under an application on humanitarian and compassionate considerations, as the appellants testified that it was the in-laws who carried out their threat with the break-in that almost claimed their lives. 18 B. According to my own analysis, the Refugee Protection Division did not commit the errors you criticize it for

The submissions regarding the errors that, according to you, the RPD committed are all but clear and detailed. These submissions seem to me to be a request to analyze your refugee protection claims anew. Regardless, according to my own analysis, the RPD did not commit the errors that you criticize it for.

When they swear to the truth of certain allegations, the refugee protection claimants are presumed to tell the truth. However, this presumption is challengeable where the evidence is inconsistent with the testimony or where the RPD is unsatisfied with the explanation for the inconsistencies.19 The RPD can draw negative inferences based on implausibilities, inconsistencies or omissions. It is the evidence overall that must be assessed.20

In its decision, the RPD found your testimony and evidence raised a number of contradictions and omissions that undermined your credibility and cast doubt on the truthfulness of your allegations of fear and risk if you had to return to Angola.21 While acknowledging that you were burgled in XXXX 2015, the RPD found that you did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that this break-in was related to your allegations.22

In its decision, the RPD set out each of the elements that led it to find that you were not credible: - Your inconsistent allegations regarding the person, the uncle, or persons, the in-laws whom you stated that you feared.23 - The difference between hearing rumours of threats and being directly threatened by criminals.24 - Your vague testimony and statements regarding what exactly transpired in your country and regarding the facts and actions of the uncle whom you claim that you fear.25
According to my own analysis of your record, the RPD did not commit the errors that you criticize it for.

I would like to add that the RPD analyzed the photographs that you submitted in evidence before it.26 It recognized that you were undoubtedly the victims of a break-in and that you, Madam, sustained injuries, but it nevertheless found that you did not establish that these events stemmed from your allegations, that is, that your uncle was coming after you because you refused to allow him to marry your daughter. As the RPD found that you were not credible regarding these allegations, it could not grant them any weight. The documentary evidence is not assessed in isolation from the overall claim.27 The weight of evidence is the persuasiveness of some evidence in comparison with other evidence.28 According to my own analysis of the record, the RPD did not commit any errors.

For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination, that is, that you and your minor children did not establish that you have a well-founded fear of persecution within the meaning of section 96 or that you would be subjected to a risk within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA, if you had to return to live in Angola.

Your appeal is dismissed.
